title: Production Operating Model
readerIntent: Understand the operating disciplines required after a Nodics deployment is production-qualified.
priorKnowledge: Read deployment preparation, security shared responsibility, and operational governance.
owner: Deployment operators and capability owners under the shared-responsibility model
summary: Production operation combines owned lifecycle signals, service objectives, capacity, safe telemetry, provider health, backup/recovery, change governance, security operations, and business-outcome reconciliation.

sections.heading: Service model
items: Assign a business and technical owner to every module capability, deployment process, provider, dataset, queue, job, workflow, publication path, client, and incident runbook.
Define availability, latency, throughput, freshness, correctness, recovery-point, recovery-time, and support objectives from business impact.
Separate liveness from readiness; only started processes receive traffic, while degraded or draining state remains visible to authorized operators.
Plan replicas, durable work ownership, reconciliation, and external supervision because OOM and SIGKILL cannot execute process hooks.

sections.heading: Observe and protect
items: Correlate requests, jobs, events, workflows, publications, imports, provider calls, runtime changes, and user-visible outcomes across module boundaries.
Monitor safe rates, latency, saturation, errors, readiness, dependency/provider health, retry/backlog, cache/index freshness, authentication denial, policy changes, and capacity headroom.
Use bounded labels and redaction; credentials, personal data, protected payloads, local paths, stacks, and vendor internals must not leak through logs, metrics, traces, probes, or BackOffice.
Keep detailed diagnostics authenticated and expose only low-disclosure public liveness/readiness where the topology requires it.

sections.heading: Operate change and capacity
items: Use preview, approval, separation of duties, activation, audit, cleanup, and rollback for eligible runtime changes.
Capacity-test the actual modular topology and providers; measure startup, steady state, bursts, queues, connection pools, memory, CPU, database/search/cache limits, network, and recovery load.
Deploy gradually, watch service and business indicators, stop or roll back on declared thresholds, and reconcile derived state after recovery.
Keep temporary compatibility exceptions time-bounded, owned, monitored, and visible in release evidence.

sections.heading: Incident and recovery
items: Detect and classify impact; preserve safe evidence; contain traffic or work; rotate credentials or isolate providers when needed.
Recover authoritative data and owned runtime state before rebuilding caches, indexes, projections, or other derived systems.
Reconcile scheduled work, events, workflows, publications, imports, reservations, and user-visible outcomes rather than assuming process restart completed the business operation.
Verify backup restoration, provider failover, credential recovery, topology restart, rollback, and incident communication through rehearsed runbooks.
Complete a review with root cause, authority-boundary correction, tests, monitoring, documentation, and tracked preventive actions.

sections.heading: Current scope
paragraphs: Nodics supplies these operating contracts, but a specific cloud production environment is not certified by framework documentation alone. Each customer deployment must complete provider, infrastructure, security, scale, recovery, and compliance qualification.

sections.heading: Complete guide: Production Operating Model
paragraphs: Production operation is the contract for running Nodics safely after the application has been built, configured, deployed, and opened for traffic.
It answers five questions:
items: What is running?
Is it alive?
Is it ready to serve traffic?
Can operators diagnose and recover problems without exposing sensitive data?
Can a release be rolled forward, rolled back, or isolated by topology?

sections.heading: Beginner Summary
paragraphs: Production operation is about trust. A production Nodics runtime must tell operators what is running, whether it can accept traffic, how to diagnose failures, and how to recover safely.
For beginners, separate these concepts:

| Concept | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Liveness | The process can answer a very small HTTP probe. |
| Readiness | The process has completed required startup checks and can receive traffic. |
| Observability | Logs, diagnostics, metrics, and audit explain what happened. |
| Rollback | The system can return to a known safe state. |
| Topology | The project/environment/server/node shape explains what runs where. |

Nodics can run as a consolidated server during local development or as multiple server/node processes in an enterprise topology. The operating model must work for both. A production-ready project should not depend on a single all-in-one process unless that topology is an intentional deployment decision.

sections.heading: Runtime Topology
paragraphs: A Nodics deployment is described through project, environment, server, and node modules.

| Runtime Layer | Production Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Project | Owns the application composition, project modules, documentation, and default project policy. |
| Environment | Owns deployment class such as local, QA, UAT, pre-production, or production. |
| Server | Owns a runnable process, active module selection, ports, provider endpoints, and process-level responsibility. |
| Node | Owns instance-specific behavior below a server, such as scheduled-job ownership or capacity separation. |
| Tenant | Owns data placement, isolation, runtime governance, and tenant-specific data behavior. |

Keep local activation and remote communication separate. `activeModules` decides what runs inside the current process. `server.*` endpoint coordinates describe where other capabilities can be reached. Do not activate modules implicitly through tenant, server URL, or request data.

sections.heading: Health Endpoints
paragraphs: Nodics exposes health probes through `nSystem`.

| Endpoint | Purpose | Security Contract |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /nodics/system/v0/health/live` | Confirms that the process can answer HTTP. | Unsecured and intentionally low-disclosure. |
| `GET /nodics/system/v0/health/ready` | Confirms that the runtime has completed required startup invariants. | Secured with `system.health.readiness.view` and gated by `apiExposure.categories.operationalHealth`. |

Liveness must be safe for load balancers and orchestrators. It returns only a minimal `UP` status and must not expose paths, provider URLs, credentials, tenant details, module lists, cache keys, or diagnostics.

In Nodics route metadata, liveness uses `publicProbe: true`. This is different from a normal `secured: false` business route. A normal non-secured route still resolves enterprise and tenant context for pre-authentication or public business flows. A public probe is infrastructure-only and intentionally bypasses enterprise/tenant request resolution.

Readiness is operational information. It may report sanitized runtime state such as server state, selected environment/server/node names, active module count, active tenant count, and readiness checks. It must stay secured because it helps operators understand the running topology.

sections.heading: Readiness Baseline
paragraphs: The framework readiness baseline checks:
Projects may extend readiness in later modules. Common project checks include:
Provider checks must be sanitized. Do not return credentials, full URLs, private paths, tokens, raw connection strings, or customer data from readiness.
items: runtime state is `started`;
a server has been selected;
active modules have been loaded;
at least one tenant is active.
database connection is reachable;
cache engine is reachable;
search provider is reachable;
EMS or message broker is reachable;
required runtime configuration is active;
required secrets are present through governed secret sources;
import/export locations or provider aliases are configured;
node-owned scheduled jobs are not running on unauthorized nodes.

sections.heading: Startup And Traffic Admission
paragraphs: Startup must complete before traffic is admitted.

The runtime state moves to `started` only after normal startup has completed. Readiness should be the gate used by load balancers, API gateways, container orchestrators, and deployment automation before sending business traffic to the process.

In a modular deployment, each server has its own readiness responsibility. A profile server, import server, event server, scheduled-job server, and content server may all be healthy independently. Do not treat one process as proof that the whole environment is ready.

sections.heading: Secrets
paragraphs: Production secrets must come from governed sources, not source-controlled files.
Examples include:

The production operating model must identify required secrets for each server and node, including authentication, API keys, database, cache, search, messaging, storage, import/export, and provider credentials.
items: environment variables managed by deployment automation;
external property files outside source control;
secret-manager integrations;
runtime secret providers.

paragraphs: Production observability should answer:
provider was involved?
configuration, provider, or data quality?
Logs and diagnostics must be sanitized. Passwords, bearer tokens, API keys, refresh tokens, cookies, authorization headers, credentials, private keys, and secret values must never be emitted.

sections.heading: Audit And Retention
paragraphs: Runtime mutation paths must preserve audit evidence:
Retention must be defined by project and environment. Local development may keep short retention. Production may require longer retention for audit, compliance, support, and incident investigation.
items: runtime configuration preview/request/approval/activation/rollback;
schema and router governance changes;
identity and permission governance;
import/export runs;
credential rotation;
operational route usage where policy requires it.

sections.heading: Backup, Restore, And Rollback
paragraphs: Production readiness is not complete until restore and rollback are proven.
At minimum, define:
Manual database repair should not be the normal recovery strategy.
items: database backup and restore;
search index rebuild or restore;
cache warm-up or safe flush strategy;
import run retry and failed-record handling;
runtime configuration rollback;
versioned or publishable data rollback;
deployment rollback;
tenant-specific recovery when one tenant is affected.

sections.heading: Release Gates
paragraphs: Before release, run:

```bash
npm run release:check -- --execute
```
For release-candidate evidence, run:

```bash
npm run release:check -- --execute --full
```
Projects with live providers must also run the guarded live-provider gates for their chosen providers, such as Redis, Elasticsearch, Kafka, SFTP, object storage, or other production dependencies.

sections.heading: Support Diagnostics
paragraphs: Support diagnostics should be available through governed APIs, reports, or deployment tooling. They should help operators inspect runtime state without exposing sensitive information.
Useful diagnostic evidence includes:
Every diagnostic surface must have an owner, permission, exposure category, redaction policy, and test coverage.
items: runtime topology summary;
active module list;
active tenant count;
generated OpenAPI artifact status;
provider maturity status;
route exposure categories;
runtime configuration governance summary;
import/export run summaries;
cache and search diagnostics;
recent sanitized error summaries.

sections.heading: Beginner Production Checklist
paragraphs: Before calling a Nodics deployment production-ready, confirm:
items: every server/node has a clear owner and active-module list;
liveness and readiness probes are configured with the correct versioned URLs;
readiness checks are secured and sanitized;
production secrets do not live in source-controlled files;
data backup and restore have been tested;
runtime configuration rollback works;
import/export failures can be diagnosed and retried;
scheduled jobs run only on responsible nodes;
cache can be safely flushed or rebuilt;
generated OpenAPI reflects deployed routes;
local-only API exposure categories are disabled;
release gates pass from a clean checkout.

sections.heading: What To Avoid
paragraphs: Avoid:
`publicProbe: true` only for low-disclosure probes;
from health endpoints;
items: exposing readiness publicly with detailed topology or provider data;
treating every `secured: false` route as public infrastructure; use
returning secrets, URLs with credentials, private file paths, or tenant data
treating a consolidated local server as proof of modular production readiness;
enabling local-only control-plane APIs in production;
deploying without a clean-checkout release gate;
using sample bootstrap credentials in production;
relying on manual database changes for rollback;
allowing scheduled jobs to run on every node without ownership rules.
